content:
# n8n Fundamentals and the Open-Source Advantage ##### When "the cloud" is not an option A healthtech startup in Hyderabad wanted to automate patient intake: form submission, record creation, appointment reminders. Textbook workflow automation. Their compliance officer asked one question that ended the Zapier conversation in thirty seconds: *"Where does the patient data physically go, and who else can read it?"* With a hosted iPaaS, the honest answer is "through a third party's servers in another country, subject to their retention policy." For patient records, financial data, or anything under India's DPDP Act or Europe's GDPR, that answer is sometimes simply unacceptable. **n8n** exists for exactly this situation — and for engineers who want more control generally. It is an open-source, self-hostable workflow automation tool: you can run it on your own laptop, your own server, or your own cloud account, and the data never leaves infrastructure you control. It is also the tool where technically-minded automation engineers tend to end up, because it does not put a ceiling on what you can build. ##### What n8n actually is n8n (pronounced "n-eight-n", short for *nodemation*) is a workflow automation platform with a node-based visual editor, roughly 400+ built-in integrations, and — critically — a generic HTTP Request node plus a Code node that let it talk to anything at all. Three properties define it: **Open source.** The source is public on GitHub (`n8n-io/n8n`). You can read exactly how it works, file issues, contribute nodes, and — importantly for a learner — study a real production codebase to understand how automation engines are built. It uses a "fair-code" sustainable-use licence rather than a pure MIT licence: free to self-host and use internally, with restrictions on reselling it as a competing hosted service. Read the licence if you plan commercial use. **Self-hostable.** One Docker command puts a full automation platform on your own machine. Eric Raymond's *The Cathedral and the Bazaar* argued that open, distributed development produces software users can actually control — n8n is a modern illustration of that thesis in the automation space. **Execution-based pricing.** n8n Cloud charges per *workflow execution*, not per step. A workflow with 30 nodes costs the same as one with 2 nodes. For complex, multi-step automations this is a fundamentally different economic model from Zapier's tasks or Make's operations, and it removes the constant pressure to minimize step count. ##### Nodes, connections, and the canvas The n8n editor is a canvas of **nodes** — rectangular boxes, each an operation — joined by **connections** you drag between them. If you have used Make, this will feel immediately familiar; if you have used Zapier, think of it as the same list but laid out horizontally with branching allowed. **Trigger nodes** start a workflow and always sit on the left, marked with a lightning bolt. The main ones: - **Manual Trigger** — "Execute Workflow" button. Your constant companion while building. - **Webhook** — gives you a URL; any POST to it starts the workflow. - **Schedule Trigger** — cron-style timing, from every minute to specific days. - **App triggers** — "On new Gmail message," "On new Airtable record," etc. - **Error Trigger** — a special one that fires when *another* workflow fails, letting you build centralized error handling. **Regular nodes** do the work: app nodes (Google Sheets, Slack, Postgres), the generic **HTTP Request** node, data nodes (**Set**, **Code**, **Merge**), and flow-control nodes (**IF**, **Switch**, **Loop Over Items**, **Wait**). The data model matters: n8n passes an **array of items** between nodes, where each item is a JSON object. A node receiving 5 items generally runs its operation 5 times, once per item — the same "one execution per record" idea as Make's bundles, and equally important to internalize. ```mermaid flowchart LR T[Webhook Trigger] --> S[Set: clean fields] S --> H[HTTP Request:
enrich from API] H --> I{IF: qualified?} I -->|true| G[Google Sheets:
Append Row] I -->|false| N[NoOp / log] G --> M[Slack: Send Message] ``` ##### Cloud vs self-hosted This is the decision n8n forces you to make, and having a reasoned answer is exactly what today's assignment is about. **n8n Cloud** is the managed option: sign up, get a URL, start building. n8n handles uptime, upgrades, backups, and scaling. You pay a monthly fee by execution volume. Choose this when you want to start in five minutes, when you have no ops experience, or when the data is not sensitive. **Self-hosted** means you run it. The simplest possible start: ```bash # Run n8n locally with Docker, persisting data to a named volume docker volume create n8n_data docker run -d --name n8n \ -p 5678:5678 \ -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n \ -e GENERIC_TIMEZONE="Asia/Kolkata" \ -e TZ="Asia/Kolkata" \ -e N8N_BASIC_AUTH_ACTIVE=true \ -e N8N_BASIC_AUTH_USER=admin \ -e N8N_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD='change-this-password' \ docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n # then open http://localhost:5678 ``` Or, if you prefer Node.js directly: `npx n8n` will start it without Docker. That `-v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n` flag is not optional in practice — without a persistent volume, every workflow and credential you create disappears when the container stops. It is the classic first mistake. The trade-offs: | | n8n Cloud | Self-hosted | |---|---|---| | Setup | Minutes | Hours (plus ongoing) | | Cost | Monthly subscription | Server cost only (~₹500–1500/month VPS) | | Data location | n8n's infrastructure | Yours | | Uptime | Their responsibility | Yours | | Upgrades, backups | Automatic | You schedule them | | Unlimited executions | No, tiered | Effectively yes | | Custom nodes / npm packages | Restricted | Full control | Self-hosting is genuinely cheaper at volume and mandatory for strict data residency — but "free" ignores your time. A server you forget to back up is a liability, not a saving. ##### Executing and inspecting workflows The build-and-debug loop in n8n is the best of the three tools you have seen, and it is worth learning properly. **Execute a single node.** Every node has its own play button. Click it and n8n runs *just that node* using data already sitting in the previous node's output. This means you can iterate on one API call twenty times without re-running the whole workflow — a genuine productivity difference. **Execute the whole workflow.** The "Test workflow" button at the bottom runs everything from the trigger. **Inspect data.** Click any node and you get a three-panel view: **INPUT** on the left (what arrived), parameters in the middle, **OUTPUT** on the right (what left). Both panels toggle between Table, JSON, and Schema views. The Schema view is quietly brilliant — it shows the structure of your data as a tree you can *drag fields from* directly into parameter boxes. **Executions list.** In the sidebar, every past run is listed with status and duration. Open one and you see the full canvas frozen in that run's state, with each node's data intact. You can even copy a failed execution's data back into the editor to debug it. One important gotcha: the Webhook node has **two different URLs**. The *Test URL* only listens while you have clicked "Test workflow" and expires after one call; the *Production URL* works whenever the workflow is **Active**. Countless "my webhook stopped working" posts are someone who left the test URL in production. ##### Common pitfalls - **No persistent volume in Docker** — everything vanishes on restart. - **Test URL in production** — see above. - **Forgetting to activate the workflow** — saving is not activating; there is a separate toggle top-right. - **Assuming one item when there are many** — n8n runs most nodes once per item; check the item count badge. - **Exposing self-hosted n8n to the internet without auth or HTTPS** — your credentials store is sitting behind that URL. Use basic auth or user management, and put it behind a reverse proxy with TLS. - **Never upgrading** — self-hosting means you own security patches too. - **Ignoring `GENERIC_TIMEZONE`** — schedule triggers will fire on UTC and confuse you for a week. ##### Your hands-on tie-in Start with the practical task: sign up for **n8n Cloud** or run it locally with the Docker command above, then build a workflow with a **manual or webhook trigger** plus at least two nodes that fetch and transform data. A good beginner combination is Manual Trigger → HTTP Request (`https://api.github.com/users/torvalds`) → Set (keep only `login`, `public_repos`, `followers`). Execute it and open the INPUT/OUTPUT panels on every node — that inspection habit is what makes n8n fast to work in. Then the mini project: **recreate your lead-capture automation in n8n** — a Webhook trigger receiving lead data, a node writing to Google Sheets or a database, and a node sending a notification. You have now built the same automation three times, in three tools. That comparison is more educational than any tutorial. The assignment asks for a written **comparison of n8n vs Zapier vs Make** on cost, hosting, data control and flexibility, plus one scenario where self-hosted n8n clearly wins. The healthtech story that opened this article is one valid answer; a high-volume internal data sync where per-task pricing would be ruinous is another. ##### Key takeaways - n8n is open-source, fair-code licensed, and self-hostable — you can run the whole platform on infrastructure you control. - Workflows are canvases of nodes; data flows as an array of JSON items, and most nodes run once per item. - Cloud gets you started in minutes; self-hosting wins on cost at volume, data residency, and unrestricted customization — at the price of owning uptime, backups and patches. - Per-execution pricing means node count is effectively free, which changes how ambitious your workflows can be. - Learn the debug loop: run individual nodes, read INPUT/OUTPUT panels, use the Schema view, and never confuse the webhook Test URL with the Production URL.
